questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had been to Bergen once before and loved the city, the university had a specialisation within political science that interested me and that Copenhagen didn't have and the university guaranteed housing through the organisation Sammen.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, I don't remember having any issues.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had some assistance logging into the university's wi-fi and got great help from the student center and university librarians.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was very easy through the website of the organisation Sammen. I would highly recommend living at Fantoft and in a flat with private room and shared kitchen with 7 others. Fantoft is a very social and international place, and is the best place to find friends. Students living at Grønneviksøren or Alrek didn't find it as easy making new friends. Do keep in mind that you might get unlucky and share your room with one other and live with 16 people in the kitchen instead of 8, and you will not know whitch one you get until you're assigned a room. As a second choice, I would recommend Grønneviksøren. Not as social, but a nice place to live. I would not recommend Alrek. The place isn't that nice, and the friends I had living there did not say too great things about it.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Living off campus is very normal in Bergen. Most international students I met lived at Fantoft or Grønneviksøren and both are off campus. And with the tram (Bybanen) it is very accessible getting to and from campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Great process, but one downside is that you don't know beforehand which courses will be available and if the courses will overlap, so you have to choose based on the courses of earlier semesters and then make changes afterward if it doesn't fit together, which might complicate getting courses pre-approved back at home.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Registration was very easy, especially for me as a student from a Nordic country. I don't remember any major complications. You do have to spend some time on figuring out how the open/restricted courses work and the order in which you have to apply, which can seem a bit complicated at first.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could easily write the institution a mail or meet up physically at the student center. They were very helpful and quick to respond to emails.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got 2/3 of the classes I wanted, and had to apply for one extra which was easy enough.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to apply for more ECTS points back at home than you need, because you might figure out after registering that some of the courses are no longer taught or that courses overlap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level is very similar to Denmark. Not too difficult, but not totally easy either.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Pretty similar apart from the fact that 2/3 of the courses were not interactive at all and there are very few to none group exercises. A lot more of just sitting still and listening. One of my courses was way more interactive, but we were also only 11 students, and I'm not sure that's the norm.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
SAMPOL205: Regions, Federalism and EU Integration
SAMPOL226: Populism and its Consequences for Liberal Democracy
SAMPOL388: Political inequality in democracy

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend SAMPOL388: Political inequality in democracy because with only 11 students, there was a lot of room for having very interactive classes and discussions. And the teacher is very nice and easy-going. You are left a lot of freedom in regards to what you want to write your exam about as well.
I would also recmmend SAMPOL226: Populism and its Consequences for Liberal Democracy as the teacher who did most of the classes is good at his job, the topic is highly relevant and interesting and the exam is not too difficult, and with a lot of freedom as well as to what you want to write about.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I was not able to rent out my apartment back at home, so I had to pay double rent. This is the amount I put at "Other fees".

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Housing was not as expensive as I had feared. But grocery-shopping is definitely more expensive than in Denmark. But I don't think it was too bad.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think there was a bunch of sports, student clubs and bars that you could join. In the first couple of weeks, they have a student organisation "bazar" where you can learn about all of them.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I don't have any particular recommendations, as I mainly got my social activities from just making my own plans with my friends.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Hiking the 7 mountains around Bergen is a must. The mountains are super accesible and the nature is absolutely beautiful, especially the view from the top. I would also recommend going for a walk around Gamlehaugen Castle and see the Fantoft Stavkirke (a church). If you can afford it, pay for a guided tour of Gamlehaugen Castle in the summer. For holidays, travel to Stavanger and do the Preikestolen hike. And make sure to watch some Ice Hockey in Bergenshallen or football at Brann Stadion. You should also go visit Bryggen. In the winter, make sure to go skiing or snowboarding at Voss.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, Danish and Norwegian culture are very similar.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Norwegians might be a bit more shy than Danes, but if you meet them at a party or on a hike, they tend to be more talkative.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None, not that big differences, at least not any challenging ones.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How much they use their nature to do hikes and sports.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Say yes to as much as possible, especially in the beginning. It is in the first couple of weeks that most of the friendships are formed, so if somebody invites you to anything, be open-minded and join. Being social also really helps on homesickness, for me at least.
2. Try to live with other people, preferably at Fantoft. It is such a shortcut to getting friends and making plans for the weekends. One of the reasons my exchange was so amazing and one of the reasons I didn't get homesick was because of the people I lived with.
3. Be sure to have the economy to go to Norway. It is a bit more expensive than Denmark, especially if you want to go on trips.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I can't think of anything I haven't already written.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living with 7 amazing roommates and getting other friends to travel with, watch movies with and do hikes with.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Coming home again. Readjusting to my old life, and going back to living alone was very tough, and is something I'm still working on adjusting to 2 weeks after coming home.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go on exchange! It has been one of the best half years of my life!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
